cities.tagline: The big one. Multiple HYROX weekends a year and the fastest-selling tickets in the UK calendar.
cities.coachSays: Closest major race to us — two hours on the train and you're on the start line. Half the crew has raced here; the other half is about to.

items.a: Depends how you want to train: 1:1 Personal Training — £180 (per month). Online Coaching — £89 (per month). HYROX Sim Entry — £35 (per event). Small Group Sessions — £60 (per month). Rolling monthly, no lock-in — details on the plans section below.
Yes — the 3-Day Trial gives you the full run of the place: sessions, open gym, the lot. Most people who try a week stay.

items.q: I've never done HYROX — can beginners join?
items.a: That's most of the room, honestly. Every station scales, nobody's watching your numbers, and Hannah will tell you the same: show up twice a week and the rest takes care of itself.

An indoor fitness race: eight 1km runs with a workout station between each — SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, row, farmers carry, lunges, wall balls. Open, Pro, Doubles and Relay divisions, so everyone can race.
We're in Stockport — exact session locations go out in the member group each week, and the site has the details under Events. Parking's never been an issue.
Session times are on the diary page and go out weekly in the group — typically early morning and evening slots so it fits around work. Check the diary or just ask.

items.q: Do you run HYROX sim days?
items.a: Yes — full race simulations with real timing and transitions, the closest thing to race day without the ticket. Members get first shout; dates land on the events page.

Yes — 1:1 coaching is on the plans. Technique work, race prep, or just faster progress than group sessions alone. Message Hannah directly and you'll get a straight answer on whether it's worth it for you.
Rolling monthly — cancel whenever, no exit forms, no guilt-trip retention script. If you leave, the door stays open.

items.q: I'm looking for a doubles partner
items.a: Post a card on the find-a-partner board — pace band, race target, one line about you. Hannah matches people by hand, because doubles is chemistry, not just split times.

copyOverrides.replace: Hannah's race-day playbook — the fuelling sections rebuilt from her own published guide. MSc Sport Nutrition; she practises what she prescribes.

Night before

Top up carbs — don't stuff your face with carbs

Race day starts at the dinner table. Hannah's rule: eat a high-carbohydrate dinner — but it's a top-up, not a stuffing. Where you'd usually have pasta, also add bread. Keep it familiar.

  • Early waves firstA high-carb dinner matters most if your start is early — fewer chances to eat on race morning means tonight tops up the stores you're starting with.
  • Not too lateAvoid eating too close to bedtime — give yourself time to digest, and don't disturb your sleep for the sake of one more portion.
  • HydrationDrink normally through the day. The goal is arriving hydrated — not carrying a litre of water in your stomach.
  • SleepYou may not sleep brilliantly — adrenaline does that. Don't chase it. Alarm plus a backup, kit laid out.

Hannah's golden rule

"Don't experiment on race day."

Race morning

Fuel by your wave time

Hannah's numbers, from her own pre-race fuelling guide: 1–4 g of carbohydrate per kg of bodyweight, 1–4 hours before the start. At 70 kg that's roughly 70–280 g of carbs across the morning — track it, don't guess it.

  • 3–4 hours outA substantial, familiar carbohydrate meal — porridge with banana and honey, toast and jam, or chicken and rice if that's what your stomach knows.
  • 1–2 hours outA smaller top-up, lower in fat and fibre — a bagel and jam, a banana, rice cakes, a cereal bar. If an early wave means you can't stomach a full breakfast, don't force one down — the night before has you covered; keep this light.
  • 30–60 minOne final small carb top-up if you know it sits well — then stop eating.
  • 8 am startNight before: high-carb dinner → 6:00 am light breakfast → 7:00–7:15 am carb top-up.
  • 2 pm startNight before: carb-rich dinner → 8–9 am breakfast → 10–11 am carb snack → 11:15 am–12:15 pm optional small top-up → 1 pm optional pre-race fuel → race.
  • HydrationDrink regularly and use thirst plus urine colour as your indicators — clear, you're hydrated; yellow, drink more. Hydrate as soon as you wake, keep it steady up to the start, and don't overdo it — a litre of water in your stomach on the line is not a strategy.

Hannah's note

"Examples only — your individual timings depend on what you have practised in training. Practise, evaluate, adjust, confirm your strategy. Then race."

Quick reference

The dos and don'ts

Do

  • Top up carbs the night before — pasta plus the bread
  • Bank sleep Tuesday–Friday, not just Saturday
  • 1–4 g carbs per kg bodyweight, 1–4 h before your wave
  • Heel-lock your laces before you leave
  • Walk the Roxzone and count your steps
  • Hydrate on waking, then little and often to the start
  • Mime the stations in your mental rehearsal
  • Gel 10–15 min before your hardest stations
  • Use thirst and urine colour as your hydration gauge
  • Hold run-one pace on your wrist, not your feelings

Don't

  • Experiment on race day — food, gels, shoes, supplements
  • Drink alcohol the night before
  • Chase sleep — resting awake still counts
  • Force a big breakfast on an early wave — eat light
  • Turn up with a litre of water in your stomach
  • Warm up sprinting; build in stages
  • Take your layer off early in a cold hall
  • Rehearse the race as pictures only — move with it
  • Gel inside a station — take it mid-run
  • Follow the sprinters off the line
